subject: histology
prompt: Serial sections follow an airway distally from a terminal bronchiole. Which new finding first establishes that the airway has entered the respiratory portion of the lung?

options.text: A continuous layer of ciliated columnar cells
Alveoli opening directly from the airway wall

explanation: Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways with alveoli opening from their walls. These openings permit gas exchange; terminal bronchioles remain entirely conducting airways.

distractorExplanations.A: Ciliated epithelium also occurs in conducting airways and does not establish a gas-exchange region.
distractorExplanations.C: Seromucous glands characterize more proximal conducting airways and are absent from bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: Cartilage supports bronchi; it is absent from bronchioles and the alveolar region.

learningObjective: Distinguish the terminal conducting airway from the first respiratory airway.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A specimen from an inferior nasal concha has a vascular lamina propria and small seromucous glands. Which pairing best explains how this mucosa conditions inspired air?

options.text: Cartilage warms the air; cilia supply water
Goblet cells warm the air; bone removes particles
Basal cells humidify the air; capillaries produce mucus
Superficial blood vessels warm the air; glandular water humidifies it

explanation: The rich superficial vascular network transfers heat to inspired air. Water in glandular secretions humidifies it, while mucus traps particles for clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: Cartilage provides support, and cilia move the mucus layer rather than supply water.
distractorExplanations.B: Goblet cells secrete mucin; warming depends chiefly on the underlying vasculature.
distractorExplanations.C: Basal cells are progenitors, and capillaries do not secrete mucus.

learningObjective: Relate the vascular and glandular components of nasal mucosa to air conditioning.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: After a limited toxic injury to the olfactory mucosa, a patient gradually recovers some sense of smell. Which local cell population provides the most direct source of replacement olfactory neurons?
explanation: Basal cells in the olfactory epithelium act as stem cells for olfactory neurons and supporting cells. This regenerative capacity can allow recovery after injury confined to the mucosa.

distractorExplanations.B: Mature ciliated respiratory cells clear mucus and are not the olfactory neuronal stem-cell population.
distractorExplanations.C: Bowman gland cells supply serous fluid around olfactory cilia rather than replacement neurons.
distractorExplanations.D: Alveolar macrophages are pulmonary phagocytes, not progenitors in the nasal epithelium.

learningObjective: Identify the regenerative cell population of olfactory epithelium.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: An uncommon columnar cell in respiratory epithelium has a tuft of short apical microvilli and synaptic contact with an afferent nerve ending at its base. What is its principal role?
explanation: This is the description of a brush cell. Its apical microvilli and basal afferent contact support a chemosensory role.

distractorExplanations.A: Mucin secretion is principally a goblet-cell function in this epithelium.
distractorExplanations.B: Basal stem and progenitor cells replace the epithelial populations.
distractorExplanations.D: Mucus propulsion depends on the motile cilia of ciliated columnar cells, not brush-cell microvilli.

learningObjective: Differentiate brush-cell function from goblet, basal, and ciliated-cell functions.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A bronchial neoplasm shows neuroendocrine differentiation. Which normal respiratory epithelial population contains dense-core granules and provides the relevant normal counterpart?
explanation: Small granule or Kulchitsky cells belong to the diffuse neuroendocrine system and contain dense-core granules. Junqueira relates small cell carcinoma to this bronchial epithelial population.

distractorExplanations.A: Goblet cells contain mucin secretory granules and are not the described neuroendocrine population.
distractorExplanations.C: Basal cells are mitotically active progenitors rather than the dense-core-granule endocrine cells.
distractorExplanations.D: Ciliated cells specialize in mucus transport and do not define the neuroendocrine cell population.

learningObjective: Identify the neuroendocrine component of respiratory epithelium.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A bronchial biopsy from a long-term smoker shows replacement of the normal ciliated lining by stratified squamous epithelium. Which protective function is most directly lost in the affected area?

options.text: Elastic recoil of the interalveolar septa
Production of alveolar surfactant by type II cells

explanation: Squamous metaplasia replaces the ciliated respiratory epithelium with a nonciliated stratified lining. The affected surface can no longer perform normal mucociliary clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: Elastic recoil is a function of elastic fibers in pulmonary tissue, not of the bronchial epithelial cilia.
distractorExplanations.B: Type II pneumocytes are alveolar cells; this biopsy describes a bronchial epithelial change.
distractorExplanations.C: Alveolar macrophages perform phagocytosis independently of the bronchial ciliated lining.

learningObjective: Explain the functional consequence of squamous metaplasia of respiratory epithelium.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A laryngeal flap that deflects swallowed material away from the airway is sampled. Its lingual surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium. Which tissue normally supports the core of this structure?

options.text: A vocal ligament of elastic connective tissue without cartilage
A circular layer of smooth muscle without cartilage

explanation: The structure is the epiglottis. It contains elastic cartilage; its lingual surface has stratified squamous epithelium, with a variable transition to respiratory epithelium on the laryngeal surface.

distractorExplanations.A: Hyaline cartilage supports larger laryngeal elements such as the thyroid and cricoid, not the epiglottic core.
distractorExplanations.B: The vocal ligament supports the free edge of a true vocal fold, not the epiglottic flap.
distractorExplanations.D: Smooth muscle is important in tracheal and bronchial walls but is not the supporting core of the epiglottis.

learningObjective: Recognize the epithelial and cartilaginous organization of the epiglottis.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: During phonation, a paired mucosal fold vibrates over an elastic ligament and a striated vocalis muscle. Which epithelium is best suited to the exposed vibrating surface?

options.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium dominated by club cells

explanation: True vocal folds are covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which protects against abrasion and drying during rapid air movement. The elastic ligament and skeletal vocalis muscle support phonation.

distractorExplanations.B: Mesothelium lines pleural serosal surfaces, not the vibrating surface of a vocal fold.
distractorExplanations.C: Club-cell-rich cuboidal epithelium characterizes terminal bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: Respiratory epithelium covers much of the larynx, including much of the vestibular folds, but the exposed true vocal folds have a protective squamous lining.

learningObjective: Relate true vocal-fold epithelium to mechanical stress during phonation.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: During a forceful cough, the posterior muscular bridge between the open ends of tracheal cartilage rings contracts. What is the immediate mechanical effect?

options.text: The tracheal lumen widens and expelled-air velocity falls
The open cartilage ends separate, increasing tracheal diameter
The tracheal diameter remains fixed because the cartilage prevents all narrowing
The tracheal lumen narrows and expelled-air velocity increases

explanation: The trachealis is smooth muscle spanning the posterior gap of the C-shaped cartilage rings. Its contraction narrows the airway during coughing, increasing the velocity of expelled air and aiding clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the cough response; relaxation, rather than contraction, permits widening.
distractorExplanations.B: Contraction of the posterior muscular bridge narrows rather than widens the tracheal lumen.
distractorExplanations.C: The posterior gap in the C-shaped rings permits the trachealis to alter the lumen; the support is not a rigid complete cylinder.

learningObjective: Explain how trachealis contraction contributes to the cough reflex.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A small intrapulmonary airway has a folded epithelial lining and a relatively prominent smooth-muscle wall. Which additional finding most strongly supports classification as a bronchiole rather than a bronchus?

options.text: Seromucous glands and a complete cartilage ring
Absence of both cartilage and mucosal glands
Numerous cartilage plates with occasional lymphoid nodules
A thick squamous lining over a vocal ligament

explanation: Bronchioles lack cartilage and mucosal glands, while retaining smooth muscle. Bronchi have cartilage and glands, although both become less prominent as the branches become smaller.

distractorExplanations.A: Glands and cartilage support a more proximal conducting airway, not a bronchiole.
distractorExplanations.C: Cartilage plates are characteristic of intrapulmonary bronchi.
distractorExplanations.D: A squamous lining over a vocal ligament describes a true vocal fold, not an intrapulmonary airway.

learningObjective: Use cartilage and gland distribution to distinguish bronchioles from bronchi.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A nonciliated, dome-shaped epithelial cell in a terminal bronchiole metabolizes inhaled xenobiotics. Which intracellular compartment is especially important for this activity?

options.text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum with detoxifying enzymes
Lamellar bodies containing newly stored alveolar surfactant
Apical mucin granules of a goblet cell

explanation: Club cells have smooth endoplasmic reticulum containing detoxifying enzymes, including a P450 system. Their other functions include secretion of protective proteins and surfactant components.

distractorExplanations.B: Lamellar bodies are the characteristic surfactant-storage organelles of type II alveolar cells, not the principal club-cell detoxification compartment.
distractorExplanations.C: Club cells are nonciliated; cilia mediate surface transport rather than xenobiotic metabolism.
distractorExplanations.D: Goblet-cell granules store mucin; they do not provide the described detoxifying enzyme system.

learningObjective: Connect club-cell ultrastructure with xenobiotic detoxification.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: An asthma attack produces abrupt narrowing of small conducting airways. Which histological feature allows these airways to change caliber markedly despite having no cartilage?

options.text: An encircling ring of skeletal muscle
A wall made only of fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae

explanation: Bronchioles have a proportionately prominent smooth-muscle layer. Contraction of this layer produces bronchospasm and can sharply reduce the lumen.

distractorExplanations.A: Bronchiolar epithelium is not keratinized, and epithelial keratin does not produce acute constriction.
distractorExplanations.B: Bronchiolar muscle is smooth, not skeletal.
distractorExplanations.D: Fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae characterize the alveolar gas-exchange barrier, not the entire bronchiolar wall.

learningObjective: Identify the structural basis of bronchiolar bronchospasm.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: After a quiet inspiration, the lungs recoil as the inspiratory muscles relax. Which component of the interalveolar septa contributes most directly to this passive recoil?

options.text: Elastic fibers returning toward their unstretched state

explanation: Elastic fibers are stretched during lung expansion and recoil during expiration. Reticular fibers provide a supporting framework and help limit excessive distention, but are not contractile cells.

distractorExplanations.A: Cartilage supports conducting bronchi and is absent from the interalveolar septa.
distractorExplanations.B: Mucin traps material in conducting airways; it is not the recoil element of alveolar walls.
distractorExplanations.C: Reticular fibers do resist excessive distention, but the passive recoil described is most directly associated with elastic fibers.

learningObjective: Differentiate elastic recoil from the supporting role of reticular fibers.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A bronchiole becomes obstructed, yet some air can reach adjacent alveoli through openings in their shared septa. Which structures provide this route?

options.text: Spaces between unsealed type I cells

explanation: Alveolar pores connect neighboring alveoli and allow pressure equilibration and collateral passage of air when a local airway is blocked.

distractorExplanations.B: Pulmonary capillary endothelium is continuous, not fenestrated, and the vascular lumen is not an air passage.
distractorExplanations.C: Seromucous gland ducts open into conducting airways; they do not connect neighboring alveoli.
distractorExplanations.D: Type I cells form tight junctions. Unsealed gaps would disrupt the barrier rather than provide the normal collateral route.

learningObjective: Explain the function of alveolar pores in collateral ventilation.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: At the thinnest part of an interalveolar septum, oxygen crosses from the alveolar lining toward capillary blood. Which sequence correctly lists the principal tissue components encountered?

options.text: Type II cell, cartilage matrix, fenestrated endothelium
Alveolar macrophage, separate thick connective-tissue layers, endothelium
Type I cell cytoplasm, fused basal laminae, capillary endothelial cytoplasm
Ciliated bronchiolar cell, smooth muscle, pulmonary venous wall

explanation: The thin blood-air barrier consists of attenuated type I alveolar epithelium, fused epithelial and capillary basal laminae, and attenuated continuous capillary endothelium. The surfactant film lies on the air-facing surface.

distractorExplanations.A: Type II cells are bulky surfactant-producing cells, cartilage is absent here, and alveolar capillaries are not fenestrated.
distractorExplanations.B: Macrophages are not a continuous lining layer, and a thick connective-tissue interval would impede diffusion.
distractorExplanations.D: This combines conducting-airway and larger-vessel structures rather than the alveolar capillary barrier.

learningObjective: State the tissue components of the thin blood-air barrier.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A student argues that pulmonary capillaries must be fenestrated because gas exchange is rapid. Which ultrastructural description corrects this claim?

options.text: Discontinuous endothelial cells separated by large gaps
Continuous, extremely thin endothelial cells with organelles concentrated near the nucleus
A double layer of cuboidal endothelial cells
An endothelial lining replaced by type II pneumocytes

explanation: Alveolar capillary endothelium is continuous and nonfenestrated. Its attenuated cytoplasm, with most organelles near the nucleus, minimizes the diffusion distance without requiring endothelial pores.

distractorExplanations.A: Large discontinuities are not a normal feature of the alveolar capillary barrier.
distractorExplanations.C: A multilayered cuboidal lining would greatly increase the diffusion distance and is not the normal capillary structure.
distractorExplanations.D: Pneumocytes line the alveolar air side; endothelial cells continue to line the capillary blood side.

learningObjective: Recognize that alveolar capillaries are continuous rather than fenestrated.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: Morphometry shows that one epithelial population covers about 95% of the alveolar surface despite having very little cytoplasm away from its nucleus. Which population is being measured?
explanation: Type I pneumocytes are highly attenuated squamous cells covering approximately 95% of the alveolar lining surface. This percentage refers to surface coverage, not to the proportion of all lung cells.

distractorExplanations.A: Macrophages can lie on alveolar surfaces or in septa but do not form the continuous epithelial lining.
distractorExplanations.B: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal and cover the smaller remaining portion of the alveolar surface.
distractorExplanations.C: Club cells are characteristic of bronchiolar epithelium, not the broad gas-exchange lining.

learningObjective: Distinguish type I surface coverage from type II secretory specialization.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A distal lung passage is lined almost entirely by alveolar openings. Small eosinophilic knobs project between adjacent openings. What do these knobs principally represent?

options.text: Clusters of type II alveolar cells

explanation: Alveolar ducts are bordered by alveolar openings with strands of smooth muscle around their rims. In sections, this muscle can appear as eosinophilic knobs between alveoli.

distractorExplanations.A: Cartilage is absent from alveolar ducts.
distractorExplanations.C: Mucosal glands are absent from the bronchiolar and alveolar portions of the airway.
distractorExplanations.D: Type II cells are cuboidal epithelial cells within the alveolar lining; the rim-like eosinophilic knobs described here represent smooth muscle.

learningObjective: Recognize the histological organization of an alveolar duct.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A pulmonary surfactant preparation contains dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine but lacks proteins needed for its proper orientation within the surface film. Which protein pair is most directly missing?
explanation: The hydrophobic proteins SP-B and SP-C are required for the proper organization of DPPC in the alveolar surfactant film. SP-A and SP-D have important innate immune functions.

distractorExplanations.A: SP-A and SP-D are the hydrophilic surfactant proteins emphasized for innate immune protection, not the specified DPPC-orienting pair.
distractorExplanations.B: Collagen and elastin are extracellular supporting fibers, not surfactant proteins.
distractorExplanations.D: Mucin and lysozyme contribute to airway defense but are not the SP-B/SP-C pair organizing DPPC.

learningObjective: Distinguish the biophysical and immune roles of surfactant proteins.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: Which components of the alveolar surfactant system are especially associated with innate immune protection rather than with orienting DPPC in the surface film?
explanation: SP-A and SP-D are hydrophilic surfactant proteins with important innate immune functions. The hydrophobic SP-B and SP-C proteins primarily support the organization of the lipid film.

distractorExplanations.B: SP-B and SP-C are emphasized for proper lipid-film organization, not the immune role asked here.
distractorExplanations.C: SP-A has the immune role, but SP-B is a hydrophobic protein involved in proper lipid-film organization.
distractorExplanations.D: SP-D has the immune role, but SP-C is a hydrophobic protein involved in lipid-film organization.

learningObjective: Identify the surfactant proteins associated with alveolar innate immunity.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: Following a limited inhalational injury, many type I alveolar cells are lost. Which surviving epithelial population proliferates and produces progeny capable of restoring both type I and type II cells?
explanation: Remaining type II pneumocytes can enter mitosis after alveolar injury. Their progeny provide precursors for both major alveolar epithelial cell types.

distractorExplanations.A: Ciliated tracheal cells belong to a different epithelial compartment and are not the local alveolar progenitor population.
distractorExplanations.B: Macrophages remove debris but do not normally regenerate the pneumocyte lining.
distractorExplanations.D: Endothelial cells repair the vascular lining, not the type I/type II alveolar epithelium.

learningObjective: Identify type II pneumocytes as a source of alveolar epithelial repair.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: Sputum from a patient with pulmonary congestion contains large phagocytic cells with iron-positive brown pigment. Which description best explains these cells?

options.text: Type II pneumocytes storing DPPC in lamellar bodies
Type I pneumocytes accumulating elastic fibers
Alveolar macrophages containing hemosiderin from ingested erythrocytes

explanation: Alveolar macrophages ingest erythrocytes that escape congested or damaged pulmonary capillaries. Hemosiderin accumulation produces iron-positive heart failure cells, which may reach sputum via airway clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: Lamellar bodies contain surfactant components; they do not explain iron-positive pigment from erythrocyte degradation.
distractorExplanations.B: Ciliated cells move mucus but are not the described large iron-laden phagocytes.
distractorExplanations.C: Type I cells are attenuated epithelial cells, not the principal erythrocyte-clearing phagocytes.

learningObjective: Differentiate hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages from pneumocytes.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A vessel follows the bronchial tree, carries oxygen-poor blood, and supplies the dense capillary networks around alveoli. Which vessel best matches this description?
explanation: Pulmonary arterial branches accompany the bronchial tree and supply the dense capillary networks around alveoli. Pulmonary venules initially course separately through the parenchyma.

distractorExplanations.A: Pulmonary venules collect blood from alveolar capillaries and initially course separately from airways.
distractorExplanations.C: Bronchial arteries also accompany airways, but they carry oxygen-rich systemic blood and chiefly nourish tissues down to respiratory bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: Deep lymphatics drain tissue fluid rather than supply oxygen-poor blood to alveolar capillary networks.

learningObjective: Distinguish pulmonary arterial and venous relationships to the bronchial tree.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: A thin membrane from the outer lung surface has a flattened epithelial lining on collagen- and elastic-fiber-rich connective tissue. Which description is correct?

options.text: Visceral pleura lined by simple squamous mesothelium
Parietal pleura lined by simple squamous mesothelium
An interalveolar septum lined by pneumocytes
A small bronchial wall lined by respiratory epithelium

explanation: The visceral pleura covers the lung surface and consists of simple squamous mesothelium over thin connective tissue. It is continuous with parietal pleura at the hilum; a lubricating serous film facilitates movement between them.

distractorExplanations.B: The histological lining is similar, but parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall rather than the outer lung surface.
distractorExplanations.C: An interalveolar septum lies between air spaces within the lung and contains the gas-exchange capillary network; it is not the outer serosal covering.
distractorExplanations.D: A bronchial wall surrounds an airway lumen and is not the simple squamous serosal membrane described.

learningObjective: Recognize visceral pleura and its mesothelial lining.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

subject: histology
prompt: Which epithelial classification best matches the lining in this micrograph? Consider the nuclei at different heights, pale secretory cells, and the luminal ciliated border.
explanation: The field shows respiratory epithelium: ciliated pseudostratified columnar cells with goblet cells. Nuclei lie at different heights, but the epithelial cell types contact the basement membrane.

distractorExplanations.A: The distinct basal population and staggered nuclei fit a pseudostratified lining rather than a uniformly simple columnar layer.
distractorExplanations.B: The luminal cells are columnar and ciliated, not flattened stratified squamous cells.
distractorExplanations.D: The epithelium is tall and pseudostratified rather than a single attenuated squamous layer.

learningObjective: Identify respiratory epithelium in a light micrograph.

subject: histology
prompt: This micrograph is from the specialized mucosa at the roof of the nasal cavity. Which cells normally occupy an intermediate nuclear zone within its thick epithelium?

options.text: Serous acinar cells of Bowman glands

explanation: Olfactory mucosa contains bipolar receptor neurons between the basal stem-cell compartment and the more superficial supporting-cell nuclear zone. Their apical dendrites bear nonmotile receptor cilia.

distractorExplanations.B: Basal stem cells lie next to the basal lamina rather than in the intermediate neuronal nuclear zone.
distractorExplanations.C: Supporting-cell nuclei form a more superficial zone, closer to the luminal surface.
distractorExplanations.D: Bowman glands lie in the underlying lamina propria; their acinar cells do not form the intermediate epithelial nuclear zone.

subject: histology
prompt: In this laryngeal section, consider the lower pair of sharper folds bordering the central airway, beneath the broad lateral recesses. Which description best matches these folds?

options.text: Vestibular folds with abundant seromucous glands as their main specialization
Epiglottic folds built around elastic cartilage
Tracheal folds supported by C-shaped cartilage rings
True vocal folds with squamous epithelium and underlying vocalis muscle

explanation: The lower, sharper projections are the true vocal folds. Their squamous lining, elastic vocal ligament, and large underlying skeletal vocalis muscle support vibration and phonation. The larger gland-rich vestibular folds lie above the ventricles.

distractorExplanations.A: The vestibular folds are the broader upper folds, above the lateral ventricles.
distractorExplanations.B: The epiglottis is a separate elastic-cartilage-supported flap and is not this paired lower projection.
distractorExplanations.C: Tracheal cartilage rings do not form the paired folds and intervening ventricles seen here.

learningObjective: Distinguish true vocal folds from vestibular folds in a laryngeal section.

subject: histology
prompt: The micrograph shows part of a tracheal wall, with its luminal epithelium above and supporting tissue below. What is the principal contribution of the clustered glandular units in the middle of the field?

options.text: Watery mucus for the conducting-airway surface
A lubricating film within the pleural cavity

explanation: Seromucous glands in the tracheal wall contribute watery mucus to the airway surface. The mucus participates in trapping material for mucociliary clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: The alveolar surfactant film is principally supplied by type II pneumocytes, not tracheal seromucous acini.
distractorExplanations.C: Pleural lubrication occurs at a mesothelial serosal surface, not through tracheal glands.
distractorExplanations.D: Odorant receptors are on olfactory neuronal cilia; glandular units do not produce sensory cilia.

subject: histology
prompt: This airway wall has a ciliated epithelial surface on the left and supporting cartilage at the right edge. Which normal intrapulmonary airway is most consistent with this combination?
explanation: A bronchial wall combines ciliated epithelium, smooth muscle, glands, and cartilage. Bronchioles and alveolar ducts lack cartilage, making the supporting tissue at the right edge decisive.

distractorExplanations.C: Respiratory bronchioles lack cartilage and are interrupted by alveolar openings.
distractorExplanations.D: Alveolar ducts are bounded largely by alveolar openings and do not have a cartilage-supported wall.

subject: histology
prompt: In this high-power bronchiolar field, the nonciliated cells project rounded apical domes into the lumen and contain secretory granules. Which cell type best matches them?
explanation: The dome-shaped, nonciliated secretory cells are club cells. They are characteristic of terminal bronchioles and contribute protective secretions, surfactant components, and xenobiotic detoxification.

distractorExplanations.A: Goblet cells have large mucin-filled apical regions and are characteristic of more proximal respiratory epithelium; this field shows bronchiolar club cells.

subject: histology
prompt: The central cell in this electron micrograph contains several membrane-bound inclusions with closely stacked internal lamellae. Which cell and function are most consistent with this ultrastructure?

options.text: Type I pneumocyte forming most of the thin diffusion surface
Type II pneumocyte packaging pulmonary surfactant
Capillary endothelial cell forming the vascular side of the diffusion barrier

explanation: The stacked inclusions are lamellar bodies, identifying a type II pneumocyte. They package newly synthesized surfactant components for apical release into the alveolus.

distractorExplanations.A: Type I cells are attenuated diffusion-barrier cells and do not show this characteristic abundance of lamellar bodies.
distractorExplanations.C: Macrophages contain ingested material, but the repeated organized lamellar bodies and epithelial arrangement here identify a surfactant-producing type II cell.
distractorExplanations.D: Capillary endothelial cells form a thin vascular lining rather than this bulky epithelial cell with surfactant-storage bodies.

learningObjective: Identify a type II pneumocyte by its lamellar bodies.
